case_studies.title: Case-Specific Rubrics for Clinical AI Evaluation: Methodology, Validation, and LLM-Clinician Agreement Across 823 Encounters
case_studies.abstract: Objective. Clinical AI documentation systems require evaluation methodologies that are clinically valid, economically viable, and sensitive to iterative changes. Methods requiring expert review per scoring instance are too slow and expensive for safe, iterative deployment. We present a case-specific, clinician-authored rubric methodology for clinical AI evaluation and examine whether LLM-generated rubrics can approximate clinician agreement. Materials and Methods. Twenty clinicians authored 1,646 rubrics for 823 clinical cases (736 real-world, 87 synthetic) across primary care, psychiatry, onc
case_studies.summary: The problem of evaluating clinical AI documentation systems is addressed through the development of case-specific rubrics, which can be authored by clinicians and approximated by large language models (LLMs). The AI approach involves creating a methodology for clinician-authored rubrics and examining the agreement between LLM-generated rubrics and clinician-authored ones. The outcome shows that LLM-generated rubrics can approximate clinician agreement, enabling more efficient and cost-effective evaluation of clinical AI systems.
case_studies.how_to_apply: To apply this approach, AI practitioners can develop case-specific rubrics for their clinical AI systems and utilize LLMs to generate rubrics for larger datasets, allowing for more efficient evaluation and iteration. By leveraging clinician-authored rubrics and LLM-generated approximations, AI practitioners can improve the validity and sensitivity of their evaluation methodologies.
case_studies.monetisation: The development of case-specific rubrics and LLM-generated approximations can be monetized through the creation of AI-powered clinical documentation systems that utilize these evaluation methodologies, enabling healthcare providers to improve patient care and reduce costs. Companies can also offer services to develop and implement these rubrics for healthcare providers, providing a new revenue stream and business opportunity.

case_studies.title: Leveraging LLMs for Multi-File DSL Code Generation: An Industrial Case Study
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on general-purpose code generation, yet their applicability to enterprise domain-specific languages (DSLs) remains underexplored, especially for repository-scale change generation spanning multiple files and folder structures from a single natural-language (NL) instruction. We report an industrial case study at BMW that adapts code-oriented LLMs to generate and modify project-root DSL artifacts for an Xtext-based DSL that drives downstream Java/TypeScript code generation. We develop an end-to-end pipeline for dataset construction, multi-file task r
case_studies.summary: The problem addressed in this case study is the applicability of large language models (LLMs) to enterprise domain-specific languages (DSLs) for code generation. The AI approach involves adapting code-oriented LLMs to generate and modify project-root DSL artifacts for an Xtext-based DSL. The outcome is an end-to-end pipeline for dataset construction and multi-file task creation, with potential implications for industrial-scale code generation.
case_studies.how_to_apply: To apply this approach, AI practitioners can leverage LLMs to generate code for domain-specific languages by developing an end-to-end pipeline for dataset construction and task creation. This involves adapting code-oriented LLMs to specific DSLs and integrating them with existing development workflows.
case_studies.monetisation: The monetisation potential of this approach lies in its ability to automate code generation for industrial-scale projects, reducing development time and increasing efficiency. This could be developed into a product or service offering, such as a platform for automated DSL code generation, with potential applications in industries such as automotive and software development.

case_studies.title: On-Device Vision Training, Deployment, and Inference on a Thumb-Sized Microcontroller
case_studies.abstract: This paper presents a complete, end-to-end on-device vision machine learning pipeline, comprising data acquisition, two-layer CNN training with Adam optimization, and real-time inference, executing entirely on a microcontroller-class device costing $15-40 USD. Unlike cloud-based workflows that require external infrastructure and conceal the computational pipeline from the practitioner, this system implements every step of the core ML lifecycle in approximately 1,750 lines of readable C++ that compiles in under one minute using the Arduino IDE, with no external ML dependencies. Running on the S
case_studies.summary: The problem addressed in this study is the limitations of cloud-based workflows for machine learning, which require external infrastructure and obscure the computational pipeline. The AI approach presented is an on-device vision machine learning pipeline, comprising data acquisition, training, and real-time inference, all executed on a microcontroller-class device. The outcome of this approach is a complete, end-to-end ML lifecycle implemented in a compact and affordable device, with potential applications in various fields.
case_studies.how_to_apply: AI practitioners can apply the lessons from this study by exploring the use of microcontroller-class devices for on-device ML applications, which can provide a more transparent and cost-effective alternative to cloud-based workflows. By implementing the ML pipeline in a compact and readable codebase, practitioners can develop and deploy ML models more efficiently and effectively.
case_studies.monetisation: The development of on-device ML solutions using microcontroller-class devices can create new business opportunities in areas such as edge computing, IoT, and robotics, where real-time processing and low latency are critical. Companies can leverage this technology to create innovative products and services, such as smart home devices, autonomous vehicles, or industrial automation systems, with improved performance, security, and cost-effectiveness.

case_studies.title: A Deployable Embodied Vision-Language Navigation System with Hierarchical Cognition and Context-Aware Exploration
case_studies.abstract: Bridging the gap between embodied intelligence and embedded deployment remains a key challenge in intelligent robotic systems, where perception, reasoning, and planning must operate under strict constraints on computation, memory, energy, and real-time execution. In vision-language navigation (VLN), existing approaches often face a fundamental trade-off between strong reasoning capabilities and efficient deployment on real-world platforms. In this paper, we present a deployable embodied VLN system that achieves both high efficiency and robust high-level reasoning on real-world robotic platform
case_studies.summary: The problem of embodied vision-language navigation in intelligent robotic systems is addressed, where perception, reasoning, and planning must operate under strict constraints. The proposed AI approach involves a deployable embodied vision-language navigation system with hierarchical cognition and context-aware exploration. The outcome is a system that achieves both high efficiency and robust high-level reasoning on real-world robotic platforms.
case_studies.how_to_apply: To apply this approach, AI practitioners can focus on developing hierarchical cognition and context-aware exploration mechanisms for their robotic systems, allowing for more efficient and effective navigation. By leveraging this approach, practitioners can improve the autonomy and decision-making capabilities of their systems.
case_studies.monetisation: The proposed system has clear potential for monetisation in industries such as robotics, autonomous vehicles, and smart homes, where efficient and effective navigation is crucial. Companies can integrate this technology into their products, such as robotic vacuums or self-driving cars, to enhance their functionality and competitiveness.

case_studies.title: Cortex 2.0: Grounding World Models in Real-World Industrial Deployment
case_studies.abstract: Industrial robotic manipulation demands reliable long-horizon execution across embodiments, tasks, and changing object distributions. While Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong generalization, they remain fundamentally reactive. By optimizing the next action given the current observation without evaluating potential futures, they are brittle to the compounding failure modes of long-horizon tasks. Cortex 2.0 shifts from reactive control to plan-and-act by generating candidate future trajectories in visual latent space, scoring them for expected success and efficiency, then com
case_studies.summary: Industrial robotic manipulation requires reliable long-horizon execution, but current Vision-Language-Action models are reactive and brittle to failure modes. Cortex 2.0 addresses this by generating and evaluating candidate future trajectories in visual latent space, enabling plan-and-act control. This approach leads to more efficient and successful execution of tasks, with potential applications in various industries.
case_studies.how_to_apply: To apply this concept, AI practitioners can focus on developing models that anticipate and evaluate potential futures, rather than just reacting to current observations. By incorporating planning and evaluation mechanisms into their models, practitioners can create more robust and reliable AI systems for real-world industrial deployment.
case_studies.monetisation: Cortex 2.0 offers a clear product opportunity in the industrial automation sector, where reliable and efficient robotic manipulation is crucial. Companies can leverage this technology to develop more advanced and autonomous industrial robots, leading to increased productivity and competitiveness in the market.

case_studies.title: FastOMOP: A Foundational Architecture for Reliable Agentic Real-World Evidence Generation on OMOP CDM data
case_studies.abstract: The Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP CDM), maintained by the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) collaboration, enabled the harmonisation of electronic health records data of nearly one billion patients in 83 countries. Yet generating real-world evidence (RWE) from these repositories remains a manual process requiring clinical, epidemiological and technical expertise. LLMs and multi-agent systems have shown promise for clinical tasks, but RWE automation exposes a fundamental challenge: agentic systems introduce emergent behaviours, coord
case_studies.summary: The Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP CDM) has enabled the harmonisation of electronic health records data, but generating real-world evidence from these repositories remains a manual process. The authors propose FastOMOP, a foundational architecture for reliable agentic real-world evidence generation on OMOP CDM data, utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) and multi-agent systems. This approach aims to automate the process of generating real-world evidence, addressing the fundamental challenge of emergent behaviors in agentic systems.
case_studies.how_to_apply: To apply this approach, AI practitioners should focus on designing and developing architectures that can accommodate the complexities of agentic systems and ensure reliable real-world evidence generation. By leveraging LLMs and multi-agent systems, practitioners can automate clinical tasks and improve the efficiency of real-world evidence generation.
case_studies.monetisation: The proposed FastOMOP architecture presents a significant business opportunity for companies operating in the healthcare sector, particularly those involved in pharmaceutical research and development. By developing and marketing a product based on this architecture, companies can provide automated real-world evidence generation solutions to healthcare organizations, streamlining their clinical trial and research processes.
case_studies.relevance_tag: AI Agents, LLMs, Automation, Healthcare AI

case_studies.title: Characterizing Vision-Language-Action Models across XPUs: Constraints and Acceleration for On-Robot Deployment
case_studies.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are promising for generalist robot control, but on-robot deployment is bottlenecked by real-time inference under tight cost and energy budgets. Most prior evaluations rely on desktop-grade GPUs, obscuring the trade-offs and opportunities offered by heterogeneous edge accelerators (GPUs/XPUs/NPUs). We present a systematic analysis for low-cost VLA deployment via model-hardware co-characterization. First, we build a cross-accelerator leaderboard and evaluate model-hardware pairs under CET (Cost, Energy, Time), showing that right-sized edge devices can be more
case_studies.summary: The deployment of Vision-Language-Action models on robots is hindered by the need for real-time inference under limited cost and energy constraints. To address this, the authors propose a model-hardware co-characterization approach, evaluating model-hardware pairs across different edge accelerators. This analysis highlights the potential for right-sized edge devices to achieve efficient and cost-effective VLA model deployment.
case_studies.how_to_apply: AI practitioners can apply the lessons from this study by considering the trade-offs between cost, energy, and time when selecting hardware accelerators for their VLA models, and by using model-hardware co-characterization to optimize their deployments. By doing so, they can identify the most suitable hardware configurations for their specific use cases and achieve more efficient and scalable deployments.
case_studies.monetisation: The findings of this study offer opportunities for companies to develop and market specialized edge devices optimized for VLA model deployment, catering to the growing demand for efficient and cost-effective robot control solutions. Additionally, the research can inform the development of cloud-based services that provide optimized VLA model deployments for robotics applications, generating revenue through subscription-based models or pay-per-use services.
case_studies.relevance_tag: AI Agents, Computer Vision, NLP, MLOps

case_studies.title: Personalized Worked Example Generation from Student Code Submissions using Pattern-based Knowledge Components
case_studies.abstract: Adaptive programming practice often relies on fixed libraries of worked examples and practice problems, which require substantial authoring effort and may not correspond well to the logical errors and partial solutions students produce while writing code. As a result, students may receive learning content that does not directly address the concepts they are working to understand, while instructors must either invest additional effort in expanding content libraries or accept a coarse level of personalization. We present an approach for knowledge-component (KC) guided educational content generat
case_studies.summary: The problem of limited personalization in adaptive programming practice is addressed by generating personalized worked examples from student code submissions. The AI approach uses pattern-based knowledge components to create educational content that directly addresses the concepts students are struggling with. The outcome is a more effective and efficient learning experience for students, with potential for improved learning outcomes.
case_studies.how_to_apply: To apply this approach, AI practitioners can leverage pattern-based knowledge components to analyze student code submissions and generate personalized educational content. By integrating this approach into existing adaptive learning systems, practitioners can create a more tailored learning experience for students.
case_studies.monetisation: The personalized worked example generation approach has clear monetization potential as a tool for educational institutions and companies offering online programming courses. By licensing this technology, companies can offer more effective and engaging learning experiences, resulting in increased customer satisfaction and revenue growth.

case_studies.title: GradMAP: Gradient-Based Multi-Agent Proximal Learning for Grid-Edge Flexibility
case_studies.abstract: Coordinating large populations of grid-edge devices requires learning methods that remain fully decentralised in deployment while still respecting three-phase AC distribution-network physics. This paper proposes gradient-based multi-agent proximal learning (GradMAP) to address this challenge. GradMAP trains independent neural-network policies for each agent without any parameter sharing, and each agent uses only its own local observation for online decision-making without communication. During offline training, GradMAP embeds a differentiable three-phase AC power-flow model in a primal-dual le
case_studies.summary: The problem of coordinating large populations of grid-edge devices in a decentralised manner while respecting three-phase AC distribution-network physics is addressed in this paper. The authors propose a gradient-based multi-agent proximal learning approach, GradMAP, which trains independent neural-network policies for each agent without any parameter sharing. The outcome of this approach is a fully decentralised learning method that can be used for online decision-making without communication among agents.
case_studies.how_to_apply: AI practitioners can apply the GradMAP approach to other decentralised control problems by leveraging the use of differentiable power-flow models and primal-dual learning frameworks. By doing so, they can develop scalable and efficient solutions that can be deployed in real-world grid-edge applications.
case_studies.monetisation: The GradMAP approach has the potential to be monetised through the development of smart grid management systems that can optimise energy distribution and consumption in real-time. Companies can license the GradMAP technology to utility providers and grid operators, offering a scalable and efficient solution for decentralised grid control.

case_studies.title: Large-scale wireless network management via Open-RAN Tandem Apps: Cell on/off switching use case
case_studies.abstract: With growing mobile-network complexity, management and optimization have become increasingly difficult. Centralized algorithms face high control-data overhead and computational load, while distributed approaches often perform far from optimally. The O-RAN architecture introduces two tiers of RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs), enabling hierarchical network-management schemes. This work proposes Tandem Apps: a pair of tightly coupled optimization mechanisms running on both controllers. We show how to design Tandem Apps through architectural and functional splitting to achieve an agile, low-comp
case_studies.summary: The growing complexity of mobile networks poses significant management and optimization challenges, which can be addressed through the O-RAN architecture and RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs). This work proposes Tandem Apps, a pair of optimization mechanisms running on both controllers, to achieve agile and low-complexity network management. The outcome of this approach is a more efficient and scalable network management system.
case_studies.how_to_apply: AI practitioners can apply this approach by designing and implementing hierarchical network-management schemes using the O-RAN architecture and RICs. By splitting optimization mechanisms into two tiers, practitioners can achieve a more agile and efficient network management system.
case_studies.monetisation: The proposed Tandem Apps approach has a clear product opportunity in the telecom industry, where network management and optimization are critical challenges. Companies can develop and market Tandem Apps-based solutions to help telecom operators improve their network efficiency and scalability.

case_studies.title: Joint Sato-Tate Laws for Transformations of Hecke Eigenvalues: The Vertical Case
case_studies.abstract: We introduce a framework within which a large class of joint equidistribution problems can be studied and resolved with effective error terms. This involves proving a higher dimensional and $μ$-analogue of the Erdös-Turán inequality, and utilizing the theory of the Hardy-Krause (H-K) variation from analysis, where, in particular, we formulate a technique to approximate a broad class of relevant functions by functions of bounded H-K variation. Our main focus will be on the vertical Sato-Tate problem for spaces of cusp forms and for families of elliptic curves over finite fields. In particular,
case_studies.summary: The problem addressed in this study is the joint equidistribution of Hecke eigenvalues in the context of number theory. The AI approach involves utilizing the theory of the Hardy-Krause variation and formulating a technique to approximate relevant functions. The outcome is a framework for studying and resolving a large class of joint equidistribution problems with effective error terms.
case_studies.how_to_apply: AI practitioners can apply the techniques developed in this study to other problems in number theory and analysis by utilizing the theory of the Hardy-Krause variation and formulating similar approximation techniques. This can involve identifying relevant functions and developing methods to approximate them with bounded variation, enabling the resolution of complex equidistribution problems.
case_studies.monetisation: A potential business opportunity arising from this research is the development of software or consulting services that apply these mathematical techniques to cryptography and cybersecurity, where number theory plays a critical role. Companies specializing in cryptographic solutions or cybersecurity consulting could adapt these methods to improve the security and efficiency of their products and services.

case_studies.title: Learning to Think from Multiple Thinkers
case_studies.abstract: We study learning with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision from multiple thinkers, all of whom provide correct but possibly systematically different solutions, e.g., step-by-step solutions to math problems written by different thinkers, or step-by-step execution traces of different programs solving the same problem. We consider classes that are computationally easy to learn using CoT supervision from a single thinker, but hard to learn with only end-result supervision, i.e., without CoT (Joshi et al. 2025). We establish that, under cryptographic assumptions, learning can be hard from CoT superv
case_studies.summary: The problem addressed in this study is the difficulty of learning from Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision from multiple thinkers, which can provide correct but systematically different solutions. The AI approach used is to analyze the computational ease of learning with CoT supervision from a single thinker versus multiple thinkers. The outcome of the study establishes that learning can be hard from CoT supervision under cryptographic assumptions, highlighting the challenges of multi-thinker CoT learning.
case_studies.how_to_apply: To apply the insights from this study, AI practitioners should carefully evaluate the limitations of Chain-of-Thought supervision, especially when dealing with multiple thinkers or diverse solution paths. By understanding these limitations, practitioners can design more effective learning strategies that account for the potential differences in solution approaches.
case_studies.monetisation: A potential business opportunity arising from this research is the development of AI-powered educational tools that can adapt to different learning styles and solution paths, providing personalized learning experiences for students. Such tools could be marketed to educational institutions or individual learners, offering a unique value proposition based on the ability to handle diverse thinker inputs and solution approaches.

case_studies.title: Green Shielding: A User-Centric Approach Towards Trustworthy AI
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed, yet their outputs can be highly sensitive to routine, non-adversarial variation in how users phrase queries, a gap not well addressed by existing red-teaming efforts. We propose Green Shielding, a user-centric agenda for building evidence-backed deployment guidance by characterizing how benign input variation shifts model behavior. We operationalize this agenda through the CUE criteria: benchmarks with authentic Context, reference standards and metrics that capture true Utility, and perturbations that reflect realistic variations in the E
case_studies.summary: The problem of large language models producing sensitive outputs due to benign input variation is addressed through the Green Shielding approach. This approach involves characterizing how model behavior shifts with authentic context, utility, and realistic variations in input. The outcome of this approach is the provision of evidence-backed deployment guidance for building trustworthy AI.
case_studies.how_to_apply: To apply the Green Shielding approach, AI practitioners can utilize the CUE criteria to benchmark their models with authentic context, reference standards, and realistic perturbations. By doing so, they can identify and mitigate potential issues with their models, leading to more reliable and trustworthy AI systems.
case_studies.monetisation: The Green Shielding approach presents a business opportunity for companies to develop and market AI systems that prioritize user-centric trustworthiness, potentially leading to increased adoption and revenue. Furthermore, the CUE criteria can be licensed or integrated into existing AI development frameworks, providing a concrete product opportunity for companies.

case_studies.title: Benchmarking Source-Sensitive Reasoning in Turkish: Humans and LLMs under Evidential Trust Manipulation
case_studies.abstract: This paper investigates whether source trustworthiness shapes Turkish evidential morphology and whether large language models (LLMs) track this sensitivity. We study the past-domain contrast between -DI and -mIs in controlled cloze contexts where the information source is overtly external, while only its perceived reliability is manipulated (High-Trust vs. Low-Trust). In a human production experiment, native speakers of Turkish show a robust trust effect: High-Trust contexts yield relatively more -DI, whereas Low-Trust contexts yield relatively more -mIs, with the pattern remaining stable acro
case_studies.summary: This study investigates how source trustworthiness affects Turkish evidential morphology and whether large language models (LLMs) can track this sensitivity. The researchers used a controlled cloze context experiment to manipulate the perceived reliability of the information source and measured the effect on the use of -DI and -mIs suffixes. The results show a robust trust effect, with High-Trust contexts yielding relatively more -DI and Low-Trust contexts yielding relatively more -mIs.
case_studies.how_to_apply: To apply this research in practice, AI practitioners can use the findings to improve the performance of LLMs in tasks that require understanding of evidential morphology, such as text generation and language translation. By incorporating source trustworthiness into their models, practitioners can develop more accurate and nuanced language processing systems.
case_studies.monetisation: The research has potential for monetisation in the development of more advanced language processing tools, such as AI-powered language translation software that can take into account the trustworthiness of the source material. Companies that develop such tools can target industries such as journalism, marketing, and education, where accurate and reliable language processing is essential.

case_studies.title: Measuring Successful Cooperation in Human-AI Teamwork: Development and Validation of the Perceived Cooperativity and Teaming Perception Scales
case_studies.abstract: As human-AI cooperation becomes increasingly prevalent, reliable instruments for assessing the subjective quality of cooperative human-AI interaction are needed. We introduce two theoretically grounded scales: the Perceived Cooperativity Scale (PCS), grounded in joint activity theory, and the Teaming Perception Scale (TPS), grounded in evolutionary cooperation theory. The PCS captures an agent's perceived cooperative capability and practice within a single interaction sequence; the TPS captures the emergent sense of teaming arising from mutual contribution and support. Both scales were adapted
case_studies.summary: The problem of measuring successful cooperation in human-AI teamwork is addressed through the development of two theoretically grounded scales. The AI approach involves the creation of the Perceived Cooperativity Scale and the Teaming Perception Scale, which capture the perceived cooperative capability and the emergent sense of teaming arising from mutual contribution and support. The outcome is the introduction of reliable instruments for assessing the subjective quality of cooperative human-AI interaction.
case_studies.how_to_apply: To apply this research, AI practitioners can utilize the Perceived Cooperativity Scale and the Teaming Perception Scale to evaluate the effectiveness of human-AI collaboration in their systems. By incorporating these scales, practitioners can identify areas for improvement and optimize their systems to foster more cooperative and effective human-AI teamwork.
case_studies.monetisation: The research on measuring successful cooperation in human-AI teamwork can be monetized by developing and licensing assessment tools based on the Perceived Cooperativity Scale and the Teaming Perception Scale. Companies can use these tools to evaluate and improve the performance of their human-AI collaborative systems, creating a new revenue stream for the developers of these assessment tools.
